examples: As soon as he saw my face, he suddenly burst out laughing.
When I replaced the batteries, the toy car suddenly started moving.
Just when I thought the sky had grown dark, it started to rain.
Children sometimes start crying for no reason.
He suddenly started singing and surprised everyone.
She began talking about the old days.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize surprise or suddenness; the speaker usually did not anticipate it.
Rarely used with verbs for long-term, planned activities (勉強し出す sounds like “suddenly started studying”).
Often accompanied by adverbs:突然,急に, いきなり, とたん(に).
The subject can be inanimate (rain, wind) or animate (people, animals).

• Expresses the sudden onset of an action/state, often hard to control.
• Often used with natural phenomena, emotions, and impulsive behavior: 雨が降り出す, 子どもが泣き出す, 彼が歌い出す.
• Has a stronger nuance than ～始める (neutral, not necessarily sudden).
• Some verbs with 出す have become “lexicalized” with their own meanings: 言い出す (blurt out an idea/proposal), 切り出す (broach a subject), 思い出す (remember – does not follow the V-ます+出す pattern).
fields.notes:
• -出す attaches to the continuative form (ます-form minus ます) of Group I/II/III verbs: 笑い出す, し出す; 来(き)出す is rarely used.
• Many combinations are natural, but avoid attaching it to stative verbs or cognitive verbs such as 知る, 分かる (×知り出す).
• In spoken language, -出す adds a sense of drama to a narrative.
explain: ◎ Indicates that an action or some change suddenly begins. Used in spoken language.
examples: 1. 雨が ふり出したから、早く 帰りましょう。
It's started raining, so let's hurry home.
2. 彼女が 急に 泣き出したので、みんな おどろきました。
She suddenly started crying, so everyone was surprised.
mistakes: Confusing it with compound words meaning “take out”: 取り出す/持ち出す do not mean “start”.
Using it with stative verbs: ×知り出す／×要り出す → unnatural.
Confusing the nuance with ～始める: the JLPT often requires choosing -出す when there is an adverb like 急に/突然.
Wrong form: ×泣く出す → ○泣き出す (continuative form).

rows: No emphasis on suddenness; a process

Gradual change, tendency up to the present
<ruby>言<rt>いいだす</rt></ruby>い<ruby>出<rt></rt></ruby>す/<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>り<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>す

examples: The old woman began to speak quietly.
Just as I started eating dinner, the phone rang.
fields.explain: ◎ Combines with the masu-form of a verb to express starting some action. Used as in「読み始める、食べ始める」(start reading, start eating).

examples: Once you've finished your homework, you can play games.
I finished reading this book in one day.
When you have finished eating, please clear away the plates.
The meeting hasn't finished yet, so please wait a moment.
Just as I finished writing the email, the power went out.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize that something is entirely finished, usually followed by the next step or marking a milestone of progress.
Unnatural with punctual verbs or verbs with no clear process (×知り終わる, ×思い終わる).
In spoken language, it is often combined with ところ/ばかり to emphasize the point in time right after finishing.

• Expresses completion of the whole action stated by the verb: “finish doing, end …”.
• Usually used with actions that have duration/a process: 読む, 書く, 食べる, 片付ける.
• ～終える is more formal and emphasizes “finishing completely”; ～終わる is neutral and everyday.
• Different from ～切る: ～切る emphasizes “thoroughly, completely used up/exhausted”, stronger than simple completion.
fields.notes:
• The auxiliary “～終わる” is intransitive (needs no direct object), but if the base V is transitive, there can still be an object: 宿題をやり終わる.
• “～終わったところ/ばかり” indicates the point in time right after completion, often followed by another event.
• For large tasks, ～終える is more formal in reports: 手続きを完了し、審査を終えました。
mistakes: Using it with punctual verbs: ×知り終わる → use 分かった/理解できた.
Confusing it with ～切る: 食べ終わる (finish eating) ≠ 食べ切る (eat it all up).
Wrong form: ×読み終わりますた → ○読み終わりました.
JLPT: easy to fall into the trap with “～終える” in formal writing; choose the nuance that fits the context.

rows: Nuance of “managed to finish”; written language
<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>い<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>る／<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れ<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>る
<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>り<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げる／<ruby>仕上<rt>しあ</rt></ruby>げる

examples: He just kept on talking.
I heard that the dog kept waiting for him to come home until it died.
He has been working at the same company for 10 years.
The rain kept falling, and the river overflowed.
It's important to keep trying without giving up.
My grandmother still writes in her diary every day.
fields.explain:
Has a nuance of “persistent/uninterrupted”, with a positive evaluation (effort) or negative one (relentlessness) depending on the context.
Distinction:Vている: simply in progress.V続ける: emphasizes duration/repetition over time.
Vている: simply in progress.
V続ける: emphasizes duration/repetition over time.
Used with an agent performing an action (transitive verb) or a natural state (intransitive verb):人が話し続ける／雨が降り続く(=雨が降り続けている).
Usually not used with verbs for things that happen once and cannot be repeated (死ぬ,壊れる...) unless the meaning shifts to “keep happening” (壊れ続ける the machine keeps breaking down one time after another).

• Expresses an action or state that is maintained or repeated over a period of time: “continue/keep V-ing”.
• Emphasizes persistence and duration more than using only ～ている (current state only).
• Naturally fits verbs with duration/repetition: 読む、考える、使う、降る、笑う、練習する,...
• With punctual verbs (瞬間動詞), it is used when understood as “repeated many times”: くしゃみをし続ける、ノックし続ける.
• Often accompanied by time/frequency expressions to emphasize the length: ずっと、長い間、何年も、延々と,...
fields.notes:
• Combines with ていく/てくる to emphasize the time direction: 増え続けていく (will keep increasing from now on).
• Causative/passive is rare but exists: 読み続けさせる (make someone keep reading), 読み続けられる (can/be able to keep reading).
• Phrases emphasizing degree: 読み続けに読む (strong, spoken language), ずっとV続ける.
mistakes: Wrong type of verb: using it with verbs that cannot be repeated in the usual sense (×死に続ける).
Confusing it with っぱなし: V続ける does not carry the nuance of “leaving as is”.
Forgetting to change to the ます-form before 続ける: ×読む続ける → ○読み続ける.
Confusing subject and predicate with 続く/続ける: 会議が続ける (incorrect) → 会議が続く / 会議を続ける.

fields.meaning: Indicates the time during which a state or an action continues.
examples: I was reading a book while I waited for my friend.
She kept chatting the whole time during the meal.
While (I) was at the restroom.
While I was asleep, we went past Tokyo Station.
The phone kept ringing throughout the meeting.
Take off your coat while you are inside the room.
fields.explain: ◎ Indicates a period or a certain span of time.

fields.meaning:
「～を実現させることを試みる。」③④のように、～の行為の直前であることを表すこともある。のように、否定の形は話者以外が主語で、～する意思が全くないことを表す。
Try to do something so that ~ is realized.
As in examples ③④, this structure can also express that something happens just before the action ~.
As in examples ⑤⑥, when the subject is not the speaker, the negative form of this structure expresses that the person has no intention at all of doing ~ .
fields.connection: V volitional form + とする とした としたら としていた
examples: That child is reaching out as hard as they can, trying to grab the toy on the table.
Last night, even though I tried to sleep, I just couldn't fall asleep.
Just as I was about to leave the house, it suddenly started pouring.
When I tried to lift a heavy bag, I hurt my back.
No matter how much I urge him, my husband won't go to the hospital.
I tried to explain the situation to my father, but he wouldn't listen.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: (be just) about to do something ⏐ explain: Used to express the agent's intention at a moment or over a short period of time. Used with short-term, everyday actions. ⏐ examples: 1. 電車に乗ろうとしたときに、ドアが閉まって乗れなかった。
Just as I was about to get on the train, the doors closed and I couldn't get on
2. あ、ポチが、あなたの靴をかもうとしているよ。
Oh, Pochi is about to bite your shoes
3. ポチは、ぼくが出かけようとすると、ほえる。
Pochi barks whenever I'm about to go out

fields.meaning:
Expresses the speaker's volition.
読もう　+　と思う／と思っている／と（は）思わない
examples: I'm thinking of thanking them.
I'm thinking of moving next year.
I went to the department store, intending to buy a present for my father's birthday.
I'm not thinking of getting married right now.
I don't have any money, so I think I'll give up on the trip.
I think I'll buy souvenirs for my friends.
fields.explain: ◎ A sentence pattern that combines with the "volitional form of the verb" to express the speaker's volition. The volitional form of the verb is conjugated as follows:
fields.notes:
explain: The first person is the most natural. With the third person, add 「ようだ／らしい／と言っている」 to show the source of information.
～と思う is soft and less binding; ～と思っている is more certain, with some preparation.
Polite combinations: ～と思います／～と思っています.
Not used directly with nouns/adjectives; they must be changed into a suitable verb (例:健康に なろうと思う).
examples: 1. 今日は早く帰ろうと思う。
I think I'll go home early today.
2. 来年、日本へ留学しようと思っています。
I'm planning to go to Japan to study next year (an intention held for some time).
3. 喧嘩はやめて、話し合うことにしようと思う。
I think I'll stop fighting and decide to talk things over.
4. 甘い物はもう食べるまいと思う。
I think I won't eat sweets anymore.
5. やっぱりこの仕事、続けようと思う。
On second thought, I'll continue this job.
6. 雨が強いから、タクシーで行こうと思ったが、やめた。
The rain was heavy, so I thought about going by taxi, but I decided not to.
7. 彼は会社を辞めようと思っているようだ。
It seems he is thinking of quitting his job. explain: Used to express the volition or intention of the agent ⏐ examples: 1. 会社をやめようと思っている。
I'm thinking of quitting my job
2. 来年、国に帰ろうと思っています。
Next year I'm planning to go back to my country.
mistakes: Using it for another person without a marker of the source of information: × 彼は結婚しようと思う → ○ 彼は結婚しようと思っている（ようだ）。
Confusing it with 「つもりだ」: ～ようと思う sounds less certain.
Attaching it directly to an adjective/noun: × 元気だようと思う → ○ 元気になろうと思う。
Confusing it with ～ようにする/～ようになる: one means “try to”, the other means “come to be”.

fields.meaning: Nominalization of i-adjectives: Aい→Aさ (高い→高さ)
fields.connection: Aい (drop い) + さ (高い → 高さ)
examples: I'll measure how long this box is.
Please weigh this luggage to see whether it is 5 kg or less.
fields.explain:
When you drop the い of an i-adjective and add さ, you get a noun meaning “degree of ~”.
おもい　→　おもさ　 weight

おおきい　→　おおきさ　 size

ちいさい　→　ちいささ　 smallness

ながい　→　ながさ　 length

たかい　→　たかさ　 height
